title: The straw the gods couldn't burn
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hook: Agni can't burn a single straw, and the gods learn whose power they were using
carry: the power in your senses is Brahman's
tomorrow: what happens when your words and your mind split?

segments.voice: The peace chants, day five. Yesterday: shruti, the sacred begins with hearing, so the chant asks to hear what is good. Today's chant asks for the ears themselves.

Exam week has its own diet: cold coffee, sleep in short pieces, and if it goes well, one quiet thought: I did that. Then there's the peace chant tradition sets with the Kena Upanishad, and it does two odd things. Before any study, it asks for the body: strong limbs, breath, eyes, ears. And halfway through, the student says: may I never turn Brahman away. Why would anyone need to promise that? The Kena itself tells a story that answers both.
screen: `I DID THAT.` → `IT ASKS FOR THE BODY FIRST.` → `NEVER TURN BRAHMAN AWAY?`

segments.voice: The chant is known by its first words, apyayantu. In plain words: may my limbs grow strong, my speech, my breath, my eyes, my ears, my strength, all my senses. All this is the Brahman of the Upanishads. May I never turn Brahman away; may Brahman never turn me away. Om, peace, peace, peace. Now the Kena's story. The gods have won a great victory, though Brahman won it for them, and they boast: this is ours. So Brahman appears before them as a spirit they can't name. Agni, the fire, strides up: I can burn anything on earth. The spirit sets down one blade of grass. Burn this. Agni rushes at it with all his speed, and can't. Vayu, the wind: I can carry off anything. He can't move the straw. When Indra comes near, the spirit vanishes, and in its place stands the shining goddess Uma, who tells him: that was Brahman. In Brahman's victory you grew great. That's the Kena's teaching: Brahman is the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, the power behind every power. So the puzzle solves itself. The senses come first because they're Brahman's to begin with. And many teachers read the boasting gods as the warning inside the chant: they nearly turned Brahman away.
screen: `ALL THIS IS BRAHMAN.` · `AGNI CAN'T BURN A STRAW.` · `UMA: THAT WAS BRAHMAN.` · then, large: `THE EAR OF THE EAR.`

segments.voice: In many Hindu homes, a book that's dropped is picked up and touched to the forehead: learning isn't only yours. If you pray, touch whatever you're studying to your forehead now. If you don't, rest a hand on it. Then sit tall and breathe into the parts the chant names: the throat, the eyes, the ears. Let each one feel lent, not owned.
The peace chants, and today apyayantu: may my limbs grow strong, and may I never turn Brahman away, nor Brahman me.
Pocket this: the power in your senses is Brahman's. Agni couldn't burn a straw without it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Apyayantu is chanted as the peace chant of the Kena and Chandogya Upanishads, before and after their study, ending in Om shanti shanti shanti. In many families students set their books or pens before Saraswati or Ganesha before an exam, and at Saraswati Puja books are placed before the goddess.

fork.setup: you aced a test you studied hard for, and your grandmother says, 'go thank Saraswati.' by the Kena's story, what's the point?
options: the power behind your mind and senses is Brahman's: you worked, and you were given the means.
your studying didn't matter; the gods decide the grade.
it's only manners; the story says the gods' power was their own.
fork.reveal: Agni and Vayu were mighty, but not on their own. the Kena calls Brahman the mind of the mind. the effort is real, and so is the gift.

original.note: Sanskrit: may they grow strong; the first word of the peace chant of the Kena and Chandogya.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chant for good health before exams.
what it means: a prayer that the senses be strong, that all this is Brahman, and that the student never deny it, as the boasting gods nearly did.
what a scholar hears: maham brahma nirakuryam, may I not reject Brahman; Kena 3–4 shows the gods close to it, and Kena 1.2 names Brahman the ear of the ear.
recall: good: what we ask to hear

chat.meaning: In the Kena, the gods boasted of a victory Brahman won for them, and Agni couldn't burn a straw on his own. Offering the work says where the power came from.

tie.story: The gods boasted of their victory until Agni couldn't burn one straw and Uma told Indra the power was Brahman's.

apyayantu.meaning: may they grow strong: the chant's first word

Kena.meaning: an Upanishad opened with this peace chant

Chandogya.meaning: a long Upanishad also opened with this chant

Brahman.meaning: the ultimate reality the Upanishads teach

Vayu.meaning: the Vedic god of the wind

Uma.meaning: the goddess who reveals Brahman to Indra in the Kena
